title.text: Vigan Empanada Stalls at Plaza Burgos

title_en.text: Vigan Empanada Stalls at Plaza Burgos

tagline.text: Ilocano street food fried fresh on the plaza beside Vigan Cathedral

location.label: Location
location.text: Plaza Burgos, around Jacinto Street, Vigan City

children.text: Vigan empanada is a signature Ilocos snack: a crisp, deep-fried rice-flour turnover filled with vegetables, egg and Vigan longganisa. The stalls on Plaza Burgos, right beside Vigan Cathedral, serve it freshly fried from the afternoon into the evening.

The name empanada may call to mind a wheat-flour pie from Spain or Latin America, but the Ilocos version is a thin sheet of rice-flour dough filled and deep-fried. The Batac empanada from northern Ilocos is known for its orange dough and filling of papaya and mung bean sprouts, while the Vigan version is described as pale yellow, thinner, crunchier and slightly smaller. The filling is basically vegetables (such as cabbage), minced pork or Vigan longganisa, and egg, and each stall makes it a little differently.

The place to eat it is Plaza Burgos, in the middle of the UNESCO World Heritage city of Vigan. It is a one- to two-minute walk from Vigan Cathedral, and along the edge of the plaza on the Jacinto Street side, stalls line up selling empanada, okoy (small shrimp fritters), arroz caldo and miki. Travel bloggers sometimes use the local term empanadahan, meaning an empanada stall area. After walking the cobblestones of Calle Crisologo and visiting the old mansions, it makes a light bite around sunset.

It helps to plan your order. Start with one special empanada at a stall to taste the crunch of the dough and the saltiness of the filling, then add an okoy. Both are fried, so a splash of vinegar or a hot bowl of soup in between keeps things from feeling heavy. The cook rolls out the dough, adds the filling, folds it and drops it straight into the oil, so even a busy stall with a long line keeps turning out fresh batches. Many locals prefer egg yolk only, so ask how the stall prepares it and order to your taste.

This entry focuses on one eating experience, unlike the Vigan entry that covers the whole city. Prices are low, but the stalls are popular, and some visitors report waiting almost an hour for an order on a weekend evening, so leave yourself time. Stalls and prices change from year to year, so treat the figures below as a rough guide only.
Thin rice-flour dough is filled with vegetables, egg and longganisa and fried on the spot. It is very crisp outside and salty inside, and it tastes best straight from the pan.
Some stalls sell a special, with longganisa and egg, and a simpler ordinary version. If it is your first time, we recommend ordering one special.
Okoy, small shrimp fried whole in batter, is the classic side. Dipping it in Ilocano vinegar (sukang Iloco) makes the oil feel much lighter.
Some stalls also sell arroz caldo (a chicken rice porridge), miki (thick yellow noodles) and a broth dish of beef offal and meat. A warm soup is a good partner for the fried food.
The stalls open from around 2 PM and are busiest in the evening. The cathedral, the lit-up plaza and local families eating together are part of the sight.
Vigan longganisa is famous for its strong garlic flavor and tang. This sausage in the filling is what sets the empanada's taste apart.
Eating both the Vigan and Batac versions on the same trip shows the difference in dough color and filling. The Batac side fits well with a trip toward Paoay and Laoag.

items.title: Half-day food route in Vigan
items.subtitle: Start late in the afternoon and finish at the plaza in the evening

children.text: Stroll around Calle Crisologo and Vigan Cathedral. Head to the plaza around
, when the stalls are just opening.
At a stall on Jacinto Street at the edge of Plaza Burgos, order one special empanada and an okoy. Going early means shorter lines.
Rest on a plaza bench around sunset and enjoy the view toward the cathedral. A warm bowl of arroz caldo or miki goes well with it.
If the Plaza Salcedo dancing fountain show is on, watch it and then head back to your hotel. Check the show times locally.
Vigan is a great city for walking, but it is hot at midday, so we suggest a break at a cafe or your hotel in between.

items.subtitle: A two-day trip from Vigan to Batac

children.text: Look around the local bakeries and market in Vigan, then keep lunch light.
Eat Vigan empanada at Plaza Burgos.
Head north toward Batac and compare the orange-dough Batac empanada. Check travel times and shop locations locally on the day.
Batac empanada does not have its own entry here, so it is only introduced as a comparison.
Buses to Vigan leave Manila (for example from Cubao in Quezon City) both overnight and by day. Operators such as Partas, Dominion and Viron are mentioned, and the trip takes about
8–10 hours
when traffic is light.
Fares depend on seat class, and sources list about ₱580 (2017) to about ₱700 (2022), so check the current fare at the terminal ticket counter.
From the Vigan terminal, the plaza is a short tricycle ride away.
Bus schedules and terminal locations change often, so check the operator's latest notice before you leave.

items.title: By air from Manila plus road

children.text: Vigan's airport is reported to have no scheduled commercial flights, so most people fly to Laoag International Airport (LAO) and continue about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by road to Vigan.
There are direct airline flights between Manila and Laoag. Check the schedule on the airline's website.
A short tricycle ride in the city is said to cost about
(older sources say ₱8–10, and some drivers charge more as prices rise). It can vary with local conditions.
A kalesa (horse-drawn carriage) is said to cost around
per hour (most sources say ₱150, some ₱200–300), and you should confirm the route and negotiate.
Plaza Burgos is right beside Vigan Cathedral, so you can also walk from Calle Crisologo.

The stalls usually open around 2 PM and stay open into the evening, and the busiest times are weekend evenings and mealtimes. For the freshest food and fewer people, go between 2 and 4 PM, soon after opening.
The November–May dry season is best for walking. In the rainy season, stalls on the plaza may cut back or close when it rains, so bring an umbrella and check local news when a typhoon is approaching.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Many tourists make the stalls crowded, so a weekday afternoon is best.
Visit around sunset to avoid the midday heat.
Stall opening hours can be irregular on rainy days.

Vigan has a wide range of lodging, from boutique hotels and guesthouses around Calle Crisologo to resorts on the outskirts. Staying in the old town within walking distance of Plaza Burgos makes it easy to visit the stalls in the evening.

There is also a knack to choosing your mealtime. The plaza stalls open late in the afternoon and are busiest around dinner, so a good plan is to eat lightly at lunch and have empanada at around 4 PM as an early dinner. Afterward, relax at a nearby cafe with Vigan coffee or a cold drink, then come back out to see the plaza at night. Most stalls serve food on disposable plates or in plastic bags, so you can take it back to your hotel, but it loses its crunch as it cools, so we recommend eating on the spot.

If empanada alone is not enough, look around the morning market and small bakeries in Vigan for Ilocano snacks and local sweets. Many visitors buy a bundle of Vigan longganisa as a souvenir, but rules on bringing in meat products differ by country, so check the rules of the country you are returning to in advance. Most empanada vendors and market sellers speak English and Tagalog, so simple orders are not difficult.

Besides empanada, try other Ilocano dishes such as Vigan longganisa, bagnet (fried pork belly) and Vigan caldereta. If a street stall does not appeal, some restaurants near the plaza serve empanada at a table. Shop names and opening hours change often, so check recent reviews on a map app.
The stalls usually open around 2 PM, so plan to visit after lunch.
Freshly fried empanada is very hot inside, so let it cool for a moment before you bite.
If you are with friends, order a special and an okoy to share so you can try several things.
Dip it in Ilocano vinegar (sukang Iloco) to cut the oil. Add spice to your taste.
Bring small bills (₱20, ₱50, ₱100). Stalls generally take cash only.
You may wait close to an hour on weekend evenings, so aim for a weekday afternoon or an early hour.
Link Vigan Cathedral and Calle Crisologo into the same walking route.
If you have a food allergy (shellfish or egg), be sure to ask what goes into the okoy and the empanada filling.
Bring tissues or wet wipes, as stalls often have nowhere to wash your hands.
Ask a vendor's permission before taking photos of them cooking, and they will usually be friendlier.
Hygiene varies from stall to stall. Pick a stall where you can see the cooking and the turnover is quick.
Prices in older reviews may differ from today's. Ask the price before you order.
Watch out for pickpockets and bag snatchers, and carry valuables in front of you.
Stalls may close early late at night, and opening hours are irregular, especially in the rainy season.
Drink plenty of water in the heat and humidity. Use your judgment about ice in drinks.
The plaza is noisy. If you want a quiet meal, eat at a restaurant nearby.
This UNESCO World Heritage city has cobblestone streets and Spanish-style mansions. You can reach Calle Crisologo on foot from the plaza in about
5 minutes
This Baroque church is about
2 hours
to the north. It fits well into a northern Ilocos itinerary.
The main city of Ilocos Norte, with an airport. It is close to the home area of the Batac empanada, which makes it a good base for a tasting comparison.
Desert-like sand dunes near Laoag. Easy to combine with an empanada trip in a single itinerary.
